doc.title: Ray Bauduc and Nappy Lamare Interview, 1959-09-09

title: Ray in the Ben Pollack band and learning Pollack's beat
summary: Ray describes Pollack's band personnel, Pollack's brush-playing beat, and the arguments when Pollack took over the drums. Ray copied his style before developing his own.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Can I ask Ray a little bit about when you played with Ben Pollock? Did he just use a stick to the director or what did he do?

Well, he used a stick on a drum, which we got in plenty of arguments about. Well, it was a funny thing. Benny Pollock had the most wonderful band I ever heard in my life. That was including Benny Goodman in the band. They had Jack Teague on and Jimmy McPartland and Big Braider's on piano. I think Dick Morgan was playing banjo and guitar there and Harry Goodman on bass. I think Al Harris played first trumpet. And the saxophone, well, of course, they had Gil Roden and Benny Goodman and Larry Binion, I think, was the first saxophone player when I joined the band. And then later on I had, oh, I can't figure this, saxophone. Anyway, the tenor man. But that was a wonderful band and that band was built around Benny Pollock. Benny had a funny beat. He used the brushes quite a bit. And when I joined the band, I had to learn how to play like Benny Pollock and make the band swing. I couldn't swing the band. It was funny, but that's the truth. And I tried to play as close to what he did to make the band sound good as I could. Well, of course, later on he used to sit in the band and he'd play especially here and there. He'd teach it himself. That's right. Well, naturally, because he was out in the front. But when the band wouldn't get swing right, the drums were right down in the front of the band, right in the middle. And he'd start beating on cymbals and I'd just stop playing. I said, well, you take it, man. Here's the stakes. We'd argue about it because, after all, if he wanted me to play, and I was a little guy, a little wiry-eyed guy, you know. So I wanted to do things too, but he wanted the band to swing his way. Well, naturally, the band swung that way and that's the way he wanted to do it. So I tried to do the best I could to copy everything that he did to make the band go that way. But later on, he finally got away from the assembly, found out that I was doing all right, and naturally I elaborated on different things that he did and went on into my own style.
